reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods
chapter_title: Placement and Design of Concrete for Drilled Shafts

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Construction of a drilled shaft is fabrication of a reinforced concrete element in-situ under challenging conditions — placement at depths exceeding 100 ft in holes often filled with water or slurry. Concrete placement techniques and materials represent a critical aspect requiring thorough planning. Mix design, means, and methods typically delegated to contractor, but all parties must understand basic requirements. QC/QA during batching and placement described here; placement inspection in Chapter 15; integrity testing in Chapter 16. References: EFFC/DFI joint task force report (2018) on tremie concrete; Kosmatka and Wilson (2016) 'Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures'; ACI 336.1 (2001).
key_points: In-situ fabrication under challenging conditions — depths >100 ft, water or slurry present
Mix design and placement method typically contractor's responsibility
All parties must understand basic requirements and characteristics
Testing for QC/QA during batching and placement described here

sections.title: Basic Requirements for Drilled Shaft Concrete
sections.body: Five basic requirements: (1) Workability — must flow readily to fill shaft completely; pass through reinforcement without blocking; self-leveling and consolidating under self-weight (vibration not possible in borehole); (2) Workability Retention — must retain workability for 4-8 hours or more for tremie placement or casing withdrawal; (3) Stability — must resist segregation and bleeding under high workability; paste must be cohesive with uniform aggregate distribution; (4) Durability — low permeability concrete cover to protect reinforcement from corrosion; high density and low permeability in aggressive environments; (5) Appropriate Strength and Stiffness — structural performance requirements met. In most cases, strength demands are relatively ordinary compared to extreme workability requirements. Mix design must address specific conditions of the project.
key_points: Five requirements: workability, workability retention (4-8 hrs), stability, durability, strength
Workability most critical — vibration not possible in borehole; must self-consolidate
Must resist segregation and bleeding despite high workability
Workability retention for 4-8+ hours required for tremie/casing operations
sections.applicability: All drilled shaft concrete mix design and specification

sections.title: Placement of Concrete
sections.body: Concrete placement must be carefully planned for dry, cased, or wet excavation conditions. Dry excavation: free-fall placement allowed if concrete directed down through center of shaft via drop chute — concrete must not hit reinforcing cage or excavation sides; flexible hose not recommended; use stiff pipe drop chute or truck chute; free-fall distances up to 80 ft without problems for dry-mix concrete (Kiefer and Baker 1994, Bru et al. 1991, Baker and Gnaedinger 1960); highly flowable tremie concrete must NOT be placed by free fall (may segregate). Acceptable water at bottom of dry hole: <3 inches deep; no substantial inflow. Maximum seepage rate for dry placement: <12 inches/hour (1 inch/5 minutes); if exceeded, flood excavation and use tremie. Dry shaft with temporary casing: concrete head inside casing must exceed external fluid pressure at all times during casing extraction; overfill to account for volume filling annular space and cavities; concrete must retain workability through duration of casing extraction to prevent arching. Telescoping casing: concrete must fill void from bottom up as each section is removed; manage extraction sequence carefully to prevent water entrapment. Wet excavation (tremie or pumpline): use 'tremie concrete' mix; gravity tremie most common for depths >60 ft; pumpline also effective. Tremie requirements: steel only (no aluminum or PVC); inside diameter 8-12 in. (10 in. minimum for gravity tremie); watertight connections; smooth interior; clean (no hardened concrete). Segmental tremie for deeper shafts — disassembled as raised. Two methods to initiate concrete: (1) closed tremie with sacrificial closure plate; (2) open tremie with traveling plug. During placement: tremie bottom must remain ≥10 ft below rising concrete surface to prevent slurry/concrete mixing; slurry pumped to holding tank for reuse or disposal.
key_points: Dry placement: free fall up to 80 ft with drop chute centering; concrete must not hit rebar or walls
Tremie concrete NOT suitable for free fall — may segregate
Seepage limit for dry placement: <1 inch per 5 minutes; if exceeded, flood and use tremie
Tremie: steel only; min 10 in. I.D.; watertight; smooth interior; clean
Tremie bottom must remain ≥10 ft below rising concrete surface
Concrete head inside casing must exceed external fluid pressure throughout casing extraction
Two tremie initiation methods: closed tremie with closure plate; open tremie with traveling plug

sections.title: Drilling Near a Recently Concreted Shaft
sections.body: Construction of adjacent drilled shafts within close proximity to a recently concreted shaft requires care. Vibrations and deformations from drilling operations can disturb fresh concrete before it achieves sufficient strength. Minimum clear distance between shafts and time delays before drilling adjacent shafts must be established. General practice: concrete should reach minimum strength (approximately 500-1000 psi) before drilling within about 5 shaft diameters. Specific requirements depend on mix design, temperature, and drilling method. Contractors should develop a sequence that avoids disturbing fresh concrete in adjacent shafts.
key_points: Vibrations from nearby drilling can disturb fresh concrete before it gains strength
General practice: wait until concrete reaches minimum strength before drilling within ~5 diameters
Establish clear distance and time delay criteria in specifications
sections.applicability: Construction sequencing for closely spaced drilled shafts

sections.title: Concrete Mix Design
sections.body: Cementitious materials: portland cement (Type I/II most common); supplementary cementitious materials (SCM) include fly ash (Class C or F), ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBFS), silica fume; SCMs improve workability retention, reduce heat of hydration, and can improve durability. Aggregate: maximum size typically ≤3/4 in. for reinforced shafts; smaller aggregate required for closely spaced reinforcement; gradation must allow flow through congested cage; well-graded aggregate reduces segregation tendency. Water: w/cm ratio typically 0.40-0.45 for good durability; higher ratios permitted for dry placement; lower ratios for aggressive environments. Chemical admixtures: water reducers/superplasticizers — high-range water reducers (HRWR) enable high slump at low w/cm; retarders — extend workability retention for long pours; viscosity modifying agents (VMA) — improve stability/cohesion and reduce segregation in highly flowable mixes; SRA (shrinkage reducing admixtures) for special cases. Self-consolidating concrete (SCC): highly flowable concrete (slump flow ≥20 in.) with high stability; suitable for wet or dry placement; gaining wide acceptance for drilled shafts; requires VMA for stability. Concrete mix proportions for wet placement (tremie concrete): target slump 8-10 in. or slump flow 20-28 in. (SCC); cement content typically 600-800 lb/cy; w/cm 0.40-0.50. Mix proportions for dry placement: target slump 6-8 in.; somewhat less restrictive on workability retention.
key_points: SCMs (fly ash, GGBFS, silica fume) improve workability retention and reduce heat of hydration
Maximum aggregate size: typically ≤3/4 in. for reinforced shafts
w/cm ratio: 0.40-0.45 for good durability in wet construction
HRWR (superplasticizer): enables high slump at low w/cm
VMA: improves stability and reduces segregation in highly flowable mixes
SCC (slump flow ≥20 in.): gaining wide acceptance for drilled shafts
Wet/tremie placement target slump: 8-10 in. or slump flow 20-28 in.
sections.applicability: Concrete mix design for drilled shafts; wet and dry placement conditions

sections.title: Concrete Performance Requirements
sections.body: Workability: slump 6-8 in. for dry placement; 8-10 in. for wet/cased placement; slump flow 20-28 in. for SCC. Measured by ASTM C143 (slump) or ASTM C1611 (slump flow). Stability: no visible aggregate segregation; bleeding ≤0.4 cm³/cm². Durability: maximum w/cm 0.45 for exposure to aggressive ground; concrete cover per AASHTO (typically 3 in. for non-corrosive, 4 in. for saltwater marine environment). Strength: minimum f'c typically 4000 psi (27.6 MPa) at 28 days; higher if structural requirements demand. Temperature: concrete temperature at placement 50-90°F (10-32°C) per AASHTO; concrete cooling or heating may be needed in extreme temperatures. Heat of hydration concerns for large diameter shafts — temperature difference between center and edge ≤35°F to prevent thermal cracking.
key_points: Slump targets: 6-8 in. dry; 8-10 in. wet/cased; slump flow 20-28 in. SCC
Maximum w/cm: 0.45 for aggressive ground exposure
Concrete temperature at placement: 50-90°F (10-32°C)
Large diameter shafts: limit temperature differential ≤35°F to prevent thermal cracking
Minimum f'c: typically 4000 psi at 28 days

sections.title: Specifications and QA/QC
sections.body: Quality control at batch plant: review and approve mix design before production; verify cementitious material types and proportions; check aggregate gradation and moisture; verify admixture dosages. QC tests at jobsite: slump (ASTM C143) or slump flow (ASTM C1611) measured before each truck discharge and when consistency changes; temperature measured each truck; cylinders for compressive strength (minimum 2 per 100 cy, plus first truck, per shift, or when changes observed). Addition of water at jobsite: NOT PERMITTED after initial mixing unless a retempering agent is specified; reduces w/cm control and may compromise strength and workability retention. Concrete volume monitoring during placement: actual volume of concrete placed should closely match theoretical shaft volume plus 5-10% typical overage; significant overage may indicate cavity or overbreak; significant underage may indicate a defect (necking, loss of concrete). Concrete volume plots are a real-time QC tool for identifying anomalies during placement.
key_points: Slump/slump flow measured before each truck discharge and when consistency changes
Minimum cylinders: 2 per 100 cy, plus first truck, per shift, or when changes observed
Addition of water at jobsite: NOT PERMITTED (compromises w/cm and workability retention)
Concrete volume monitoring: actual vs. theoretical volume — significant differences indicate anomalies
Significant volume overage: possible cavity or overbreak
Significant volume underage: possible necking or concrete loss
sections.applicability: Concrete quality control and quality assurance during production and placement

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter described concrete placement techniques for dry, cased, and wet drilled shaft excavations; and design of concrete mixes for the unique requirements of drilled shaft construction. Key requirements: workability and workability retention; stability against segregation; durability; appropriate strength. Mix design tools: SCMs, HRWR, VMA, retarders, SCC technology. Volume monitoring and slump testing are critical QC tools during construction.
